topic_and_scope: Assessment of neonatal mortality determinants in Luuka district, Uganda, using verbal and social autopsy data to identify causes, settings, and health-system barriers over 2017–2019, with a focus on delays in care and facility readiness.
main_themes: Delays in care-seeking and access to services (three-delay model: delay 1, delay 2, delay 3)
Health facility readiness, supplies, and workforce capacity for newborn care
Community and health-system factors, including TBAs, cultural beliefs, transportation, and costs
main_findings: Birth asphyxia was the leading immediate cause of neonatal death (42.4%), followed by low birth weight/prematurity (18.6%) and neonatal sepsis (9.3%), with most deaths occurring in the early neonatal period (0–6 days).

Delays in care were substantial: 51.2% of deaths were linked to delay 3 (receiving care at facilities), 44.2% to delay 1 (deciding to seek care), and 4.7% to delay 2 (reaching the facility). Qualitative data highlighted inadequate awareness of danger signs, reliance on traditional birth attendants, transportation barriers, and shortages of essential drugs, equipment, and skilled personnel as key drivers of these delays.

key_gaps.description: No district-wide VASA deployment for newborns in Uganda has been conducted; limited district-level VASA data exist, hindering population-level understanding of neonatal deaths and actionable health-system gaps.

The study’s sample (172 deaths over 3 years) and reliance on recall limit generalizability and may introduce bias; there is a need for broader, prospective, multi-district data to validate findings and guide scalable interventions.

future_directions.title: Implement and evaluate community-based neonatal danger sign education with partner engagement to reduce delay 1
future_directions.rationale: The study found that delays in deciding to seek care (delay 1) were the largest contributor to neonatal mortality and were driven by low danger-sign awareness and male-partner decision-making dynamics. A structured program led by community health workers focusing on recognizable danger signs, timely care-seeking, and active involvement of spouses could shorten the decision-to-care interval. Next steps should include designing a culturally appropriate education package, piloting it in select subcounties with CHW training, and measuring changes in time-to-care and neonatal outcomes using pre-post designs or a cluster randomized approach.

future_directions.title: Strengthen district-level transportation and referral systems to cut delay 2 and improve time-to-facility access
future_directions.rationale: Transportation barriers and long distances to higher-level facilities were implicated in delays reaching care. A multi-pronged plan—establishing reliable emergency transport options (ambulances or community-owned vehicles), subsidizing transport costs at night, and implementing clear, standardized referral protocols with feedback loops—could reduce delay 2. Concrete steps include mapping transport gaps, piloting a voucher/vehicle-swap model, and tracking referral-to-facility times and neonatal outcomes.

future_directions.title: Upgrade health facility readiness for newborn care across HC IIIs/IVs with focused training and space optimization
future_directions.rationale: Delay 3 was driven by lack of equipment, essential drugs, space, and skilled staff. Investments should target ensuring resuscitation equipment, oxygen systems, essential newborn care supplies, and functional guidelines; plus dedicated neonatal care space to enable kangaroo care and observation. A training program (e.g., Helping Babies Breathe, essential newborn care) coupled with MPDSR implementation and periodic facility audits will help elevate care quality. A phased rollout with before/after assessments and selected facility-level control comparisons is advised.

future_directions.title: Regulate and strengthen quality control in private facilities delivering neonatal care
future_directions.rationale: The majority of neonatal deaths occurred in private facilities, highlighting concerns about quality and standardization. Policy should include licensing, regular inspections, mandatory reporting of neonatal outcomes, and participation in quality improvement collaboratives. Concrete actions include developing minimum standards for newborn care, tying compliance to facility incentives or accreditation, and evaluating impact on neonatal mortality and process metrics across private settings.

future_directions.title: Integrate traditional birth attendants (TBAs) into the formal health system with supervision and safe-delivery pathways
future_directions.rationale: TBAs continue to play a role in deliveries in this rural district. A structured integration plan—training TBAs in essential newborn care, infection prevention, and rapid referral to facilities; supplying clean delivery kits; and establishing supervision and referral links—could reduce risk during home or TBA-associated births. Next steps include pilot integration in select subcounties, monitoring adherence to safety protocols, and comparing neonatal outcomes with standard birth-attendance models.

future_directions.title: Target cord care, infection prevention, and sepsis reduction through community and facility programs
future_directions.rationale: Neonatal sepsis contributed to mortality and may be linked to cord care practices and hygiene gaps. Programs should promote clean delivery environments, chlorhexidine cord care where appropriate, sterilized equipment, and breastfeeding-supportive care to reduce infection risk. Steps include distributing clean delivery kits, training birth attendants and mothers on hygiene, and measuring sepsis rates and antibiotic use in both community and facility settings.

future_directions.title: Expand VASA-based surveillance to multiple districts and implement prospective evaluation of interventions
future_directions.rationale: To generalize findings and inform scale-up, a multi-district VASA program with prospective data collection is needed. This should pair with implementation research to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed interventions (education, transport, facility readiness, TBA integration, private-sector quality improvements) using robust designs (stepped-wedge, cluster RCTs, or controlled before-after studies). Outcomes of interest include 3-delay metrics, cause-specific mortality, and health-system process indicators, enabling scalable policy guidance.
